title: Frank's Pretty Woman

jokes.text: We're adopting a dog-fighting pit bull. We're gonna keep it in the bar.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what they're talking about, implying a normal conversation is happening.
jokes.punchline: They are casually adopting a dog-fighting pit bull to keep in their bar.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cold open energy — the casual delivery of an insane premise is the joke. Efficient and character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We're adopting a dog-fighting pit bull. We're gonna keep it in the bar, all right?

jokes.text: Because last time we tried to get a junkyard dog, we wound up getting a junkyard cat, and that's exactly where you're gonna go with it.
jokes.setup: Mac/Dennis explain why Dennis wasn't consulted about the pit bull.
jokes.punchline: The reason is a previous failed attempt to get a junkyard dog that resulted in a junkyard cat — implying Dennis always derails plans into something softer/stupider.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — implies a whole offscreen adventure about a 'junkyard cat' and preemptively shuts Dennis down. 'That's exactly where you're gonna go with it' is a sharp line that doubles as meta commentary on Dennis's personality.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Because last time we tried to get a junkyard dog, we wound up getting a junkyard cat

jokes.text: We're going to rehabilitate the dog, okay? We don't want it to attack other dogs. Now we would like for it to attack people.
jokes.setup: 'Rehabilitate' implies humane, responsible pet ownership.
jokes.punchline: The rehabilitation goal is specifically to redirect aggression from dogs to people.
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion — 'rehabilitate' sets up responsible-sounding language, then immediately inverts it. The pivot is fast, well-structured, and deeply character-consistent. One of the stronger jokes in the cold open.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We don't want it to attack other dogs. Now we would like for it to attack people.

jokes.text: If it attacks a person, great! And, if the dog-- or when the dog-- bites a customer, that person then can go home and have a great story for their friends. It's a win-win for everybody.
jokes.setup: The gang is rationalizing a dog that bites customers.
jokes.punchline: Being bitten by a pit bull in a bar is framed as a customer benefit — a great story.
jokes.explanation: The 'win-win' framing applied to customer injury is a perfect encapsulation of the gang's sociopathic business logic. The self-correction from 'if' to 'when' is a small but sharp comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You can go, like, 'Dude, I got bit a pit bull in a bar.' In Paddy's! It was awesome!

jokes.text: You can go, like, 'Dude, I got bit by a pit bull in a bar. In Paddy's! It was awesome!'
jokes.setup: The gang continues selling the idea that being bitten is a benefit.
jokes.punchline: Charlie enthusiastically voice-acts the customer's delight at being mauled, specifically name-dropping their own bar.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest performance of the excited customer sells the joke. 'In Paddy's!' adds a funny layer of brand pride in an absurd context.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Just a dial tone now. She just hung up on me, for some reason.

jokes.text: She just hung up on me, for some reason.
jokes.setup: Charlie has been on the phone with the shelter while the gang loudly explains they want a pit bull to bite customers and intruders.
jokes.punchline: He reports that the shelter hung up on him, apparently oblivious to why.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical punchline. The 'for some reason' is doing enormous work — it completes the cold open and encapsulates Charlie's obliviousness. Everything before it was setup. This is elite sitcom button-writing.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That woman seems like a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's because she is.

jokes.text: That woman seems like a prostitute. / That's because she is.
jokes.setup: Mac observes that Frank's new girlfriend looks like a prostitute.
jokes.punchline: Frank confirms it without any defensiveness or shame.
jokes.explanation: Classic two-line exchange. The humor is entirely in Frank's flat, unapologetic confirmation. Economy is near-perfect — four words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm gonna make that whore my wife.

jokes.text: I'm gonna make that whore my wife.
jokes.setup: Frank has just confirmed Roxy is a prostitute.
jokes.punchline: His romantic ambition, stated with complete sincerity using dehumanizing language.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The juxtaposition of 'whore' and 'wife' in a genuinely romantic declaration is perfectly Frank — gross, sincere, and deeply character-specific. High quotability. Only Frank Reynolds says this line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What the hell...?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Are they...?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, no!

jokes.text: Roxy's chaotic entrance — the gang reacts in horror and disgust to something she does offscreen ('You did not just do that'). She announces the place is a 'shit hole' and storms out.
jokes.setup: Roxy is introduced as Frank's girlfriend and waits in the back.
jokes.punchline: Her entrance involves an action so offensive that the entire gang — not known for being easily offended — recoils in shock.
jokes.explanation: The joke is partly visual (we don't know what she does) and partly the gang's outsized reaction. 'That broad is a live wire' and her calling the bar a shit hole while storming out establishes her as a chaos agent immediately. Rewatch bonus because the visual action is funnier than any line.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That-that broad is a live wire.

dialogue.speaker: Roxy
dialogue.line: I'm goin' outside, 'cause this place is shit hole!

jokes.text: What are you cocks lookin' at?
jokes.setup: Roxy has stormed out of the bar; the gang presumably watches her go.
jokes.punchline: Her parting shot — an aggressively crude insult delivered to the group.
jokes.explanation: Pure character establishment — brutal economy, fully in voice for Roxy. Not particularly original but lands clean.

dialogue.speaker: Roxy
dialogue.line: What are you cocks lookin' at?

jokes.text: Frank... that woman is unspeakably crass.
jokes.setup: Roxy has just yelled 'What are you cocks lookin' at?' at the group.
jokes.punchline: Dennis responds with a formal, almost Victorian understatement — 'unspeakably crass' — which is both accurate and hilariously inadequate.
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — his prim outrage at vulgarity while being a terrible person himself. 'Unspeakably crass' is funny precisely because it's so measured against what just happened.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: But she's still plowing other dudes. In fact, Tiger Woods has been calling her lately.

jokes.text: In fact, Tiger Woods has been calling her lately.
jokes.setup: The gang debates whether Roxy is worth marrying since she's still seeing other clients.
jokes.punchline: Mac drops that Tiger Woods is one of her clients — a surreal real-world name that contextualizes her clientele and obliquely references Tiger's real-life scandal.
jokes.explanation: The Tiger Woods name-drop lands because it's both absurdist and a winking reference to his real scandal. It escalates Roxy's status while being deeply weird. Pays off later in the episode when a fake Tiger Woods appears.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Someone love Frank for who he is? Come on!

jokes.text: Someone love Frank for who he is? Come on!
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Frank could find someone who loves him for who he is.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately and flatly shoots down the concept that anyone could love Frank for his personality.
jokes.explanation: Funny because it's delivered by someone who is also terrible, about someone they ostensibly care about. The gang's total lack of filter makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The other day, we were hanging out under the bridge; we found box of denim, and I'm, like, 'You know, these look like good jeans in here,' and he's, like, 'You want to split it with me, 50-50?'

jokes.text: The other day, we were hanging out under the bridge; we found a box of denim, and I'm like, 'You know, these look like good jeans in here,' and he's like, 'You want to split it with me, 50-50?' I mean, that's a nice thing to do.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what good qualities Frank has.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's evidence of Frank's niceness is that they split a box of denim they found under a bridge — which reveals their entire lifestyle in one anecdote.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Charlie's attempt to defend Frank inadvertently reveals that they both live like feral people — hanging out under bridges, finding denim, boiling it. The specificity of 'a box of denim' is perfect absurdist detail. The earnestness makes it devastating. Only Charlie could tell this story and think it's a compliment. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy anchor — a character revealing their entire life through one seemingly innocent anecdote.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie! Stop wearing clothes you find washing up under bridges.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, they're boiled, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah! We boil all our denim.

jokes.text: I wanted you to have half of that denim. / He shared half the jeans.
jokes.setup: Charlie has told the bridge/denim story as evidence of Frank's generosity.
jokes.punchline: Frank and Charlie both confirm it with complete sincerity — Frank earnest about his generosity, Charlie summarizing it like a court reporter.
jokes.explanation: The double confirmation — Frank's sincere 'I wanted you to have half' and Charlie's bureaucratic 'he shared half the jeans' — escalates joke 14 perfectly. Both characters are playing it completely straight, which is what makes it so funny. High rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mac, you look bad. Really, really bad. You look fat as shit!

jokes.text: Stop wearing clothes you find washing up under bridges. / Oh, they're boiled, yeah. / Yeah, we boil all our denim.
jokes.setup: Dennis reacts in horror to the bridge denim story.
jokes.punchline: Charlie and Frank's defense is that they boil all found denim — which answers none of Dennis's concerns and raises far more questions.
jokes.explanation: 'We boil all our denim' is a perfect escalating punchline that implies this is a regular practice with established protocol. The word 'all' does the heavy lifting — it's not a one-time thing, it's their system. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Among the top jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mass. Fat. Muscle.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Let's be clear: fat. It's fat.

jokes.text: Hey, there is some dirty crack whore in the alley, blowing the busboy from the restaurant down the street.
jokes.setup: The gang is debating Frank's relationship and the morality of prostitution.
jokes.punchline: Mac interrupts with a completely non-sequitur news report about street activity outside, delivered as casually as a weather update.
jokes.explanation: Works as a tone-setter for the neighborhood and a comic non-sequitur. The specificity ('the busboy from the restaurant down the street') adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We're becoming the Gross Crew. The Gross Crew?! The Gross Crew.

jokes.text: This is exactly why we need that dog.
jokes.setup: Mac reports a sex act happening in the alley.
jokes.punchline: Dennis connects this back to the opening pit bull plan — as if a dog would solve this specific problem in this specific way.
jokes.explanation: Quick, tight callback that also reveals the gang's deranged problem-solving logic: everything is solved by the attack dog. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I went from a tiny twink to the muscle-bound freak you see before you.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're not helping my argument.

jokes.text: Mac, you look bad. Really, really bad. What? Yeah, is that your shirt or my shirt? That's, like, way too small for you. You look fat as shit!
jokes.setup: Mac is standing there normally while Frank/Dennis examine him.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a completely savage, unsolicited body-shaming attack on Mac.
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — brutal honesty delivered without warmth. Works because it sets up the season-long weight plot. The shirt-ownership question adds a funny specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This is a chimichanga. You are becoming a chimichanga!

jokes.text: Mac, you have gained, I mean, 50 pounds of fat. / Mass. / Fat. / Muscle. / Let's be clear: fat. / It's fat.
jokes.setup: Dennis accuses Mac of gaining weight; Mac deflects with euphemisms.
jokes.punchline: The rapid-fire exchange — fat/mass/fat/muscle/fat/fat — with multiple characters ganging up on Mac's delusion is an escalating comic rhythm.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic rhythm. The monosyllabic back-and-forth compresses the whole argument into a percussive beat. Mac's self-delusion vs. everyone's flat rejection is classic Always Sunny dynamic. The structure is nearly musical.

dialogue.speaker: Roxy
dialogue.line: Shut up, baby dick.

jokes.text: We're becoming the Gross Crew. / The Gross Crew?! / The Gross Crew. / And I don't like that.
jokes.setup: Dennis catalogs the group's problems: Mac is fat, Frank is marrying a hooker.
jokes.punchline: Dennis coins the phrase 'the Gross Crew' — which is both accurate and deeply ironic given that Dennis is also a terrible person.
jokes.explanation: The 'Gross Crew' label is funny because it's Dennis — himself a psychopath — trying to enforce standards. The repetition and Mac's incredulous echo sell the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, you're already in your second act. We're all in our second acts-- don't you see that?

jokes.text: What if we took a Pretty Woman and threw it Roxy's way? / That was a bullshit movie. People don't change like that.
jokes.setup: The group discusses fixing up Roxy.
jokes.punchline: Dee proposes a Pretty Woman makeover; Frank dismisses the movie's premise as unrealistic — which is funny because (a) it's true, and (b) the episode then proceeds to try it anyway.
jokes.explanation: Smart meta joke — the episode announces its own premise and immediately has a character call it bullshit. Frank's cynicism is correct, which makes the whole episode a dark subversion of the movie template. The title is in the episode title for extra meta flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: your first act was-was shit, and that's why you're so desperate for things to be different. But they rarely ever do get different. If anything-- God, they get worse.

jokes.text: People change, Frank. Look at me. I went from a tiny twink to the muscle-bound freak you see before you.
jokes.setup: Frank says people don't change; Mac argues they do.
jokes.punchline: Mac's evidence of positive change is that he went from 'tiny twink' to 'muscle-bound freak' — which (a) contains loaded terminology, (b) is objectively false given his current weight, and (c) inadvertently undermines Dee's argument.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. 'Tiny twink to muscle-bound freak' is specifically Mac — it's self-aggrandizing, sexually coded (accidentally or not, given the show's running Mac-is-closeted gag), and completely undermined by his current physical state. Dee's reaction ('You're not helping my argument') is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He got salsa on his shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What's that smell?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Crack.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That is crack rock. She's smoking crack!

jokes.text: You're not helping my argument.
jokes.setup: Mac has just described his transformation from 'tiny twink to muscle-bound freak' as evidence that people can change.
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat acknowledgment that Mac has only made things worse.
jokes.explanation: Clean button on Mac's self-sabotaging testimony. Good economy, perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: the man is carrying around trash bags filled with Mexican foods. What's that smell?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Crack. That is crack rock.

jokes.text: If you're gonna chime in, please don't do it with a mouthful of burrito. / This is a chimichanga. / You are becoming a chimichanga!
jokes.setup: Mac is eating while trying to participate in the conversation.
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects the food item, then immediately uses it as an insult about Mac's body.
jokes.explanation: 'You are becoming a chimichanga' is a genuinely great insult — specific, escalating, and using the detail Mac himself provided. The two-beat structure (correction then weaponization) is tight. High quotability. This is memorable writing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I signed you up on a dating Web site. I got you a date, dude! This girl does think she's meeting a millionaire.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Why'd you say that, Charlie?

jokes.text: Tomorrow night, I am proposing to that dirty whore.
jokes.setup: Frank gives the group 24 hours to do whatever they need.
jokes.punchline: He announces his marriage proposal plan using the phrase 'dirty whore' with complete romantic sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the earlier romantic declaration, maintaining Frank's total lack of irony. 'Dirty whore' as a term of endearment is entirely Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: A night with a limo driver? This is a good idea.

jokes.text: This is gonna be a little bit harder than we thought. This woman is a real piece of shit.
jokes.setup: Dee and Dennis approach Roxy for a Pretty Woman makeover.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a frank assessment of the subject of their goodwill project.
jokes.explanation: Good delivery joke. 'Real piece of shit' spoken clinically while trying to help someone is very Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Whoa! I burned myself on a rivet.

jokes.text: Shut up, baby dick.
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Roxy they want to teach her some manners.
jokes.punchline: Roxy responds to a lesson in manners with 'shut up, baby dick' — the perfect ironic response.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic timing — she is being told about manners and immediately deploys the most unmannerly possible response. 'Baby dick' as a dismissive insult is specifically Roxy. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't eat lunch anymore, for instance. Yeah, and on odd days, I don't eat breakfast.

jokes.text: All right, well, I'm out of here.
jokes.setup: Roxy says 'shut up, baby dick' in response to Dennis's attempt to help her.
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately abandons the entire project.
jokes.explanation: The speed of Dennis's retreat is the joke — no negotiation, no processing, just immediate exit. Character-consistent cowardice.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I call them hummingbirds. And although I seem relaxed, I'm actually incredibly tense at all times.

jokes.text: I'm gearing up to get into my second act, you know? And that's very exciting for me. And I'd like to help Roxy do the same thing.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are supposed to be helping Roxy. Dee positions this as mentorship.
jokes.punchline: Dee co-opts Roxy's makeover as an opportunity for her own self-improvement fantasy — revealing her own desperation more than any concern for Roxy.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee — she makes everything about herself while being completely unaware that she's doing it. The 'second act' framing is both sad and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And although I seem relaxed, I'm actually incredibly tense at all times.

jokes.text: No... no, no, Dee. / Me? / Yeah. We're all in our second acts -- don't you see that? / ...your first act was shit, and that's why you're so desperate for things to be different.
jokes.setup: Dee is excited about her 'second act.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the brutal truth that Dee is already in her second act — and her first act was terrible.
jokes.explanation: Lands as genuine cruelty that happens to be funny. Dennis's insight is accurate and devastating — Dee's optimism is pathetic. The show's dark undertone is fully present here.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Stop cultivating and start harvesting.

jokes.text: I mean, look at Mac. / I got salsa on my shirt. / He got salsa on his shirt.
jokes.setup: Dennis is making a point about how things get worse, using Mac as his example.
jokes.punchline: Mac's contribution to this analysis of his decline is to report, completely neutrally, that he has salsa on his shirt — and Dennis simply echoes it as evidence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. Mac's oblivious self-report ('I got salsa on my shirt') and Dennis's dry repetition as confirmation of his decline ('he got salsa on his shirt') is tight, economical, and deeply in character for both. The rhythm is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: You have type 2 adult-onset diabetes.

jokes.text: The man is carrying around trash bags filled with Mexican foods.
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining why he needs to take Mac away to deal with his health.
jokes.punchline: The specific detail that Mac carries trash bags full of Mexican food as a lifestyle choice.
jokes.explanation: 'Trash bags filled with Mexican foods' is a brilliant specific detail — the plural 'foods' and the trash bag delivery system paint a vivid, absurd picture. This is visual comedy through dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dude, stop saying 'diabetes!' You sound like an ass...

jokes.text: What's that smell? / Crack. / That is crack rock. / Mm-hmm. / She's smoking crack! / Oh, she's smoking crack. / Okay, she's smoking crack.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are trying to leave; there is a strange smell.
jokes.punchline: The staged, almost procedural identification and confirmation of crack cocaine use — each character processing it at their own pace.
jokes.explanation: The cascading confirmation structure — four people each separately processing 'she's smoking crack' — is funny through repetition and rhythm. 'Okay, she's smoking crack' as the final resigned acceptance is the best beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm not as strong as I thought, Dennis. I've hurt my back.

jokes.text: I signed you up on a dating Web site. I got you a date, dude! / Yeah? / Check it out, though. I got a little twist on this date. This girl does think she's meeting a millionaire.
jokes.setup: Charlie announces he's set Frank up on a date — good news.
jokes.punchline: The 'twist' is that he's already told the woman Frank is a millionaire — which defeats the entire purpose of a genuine connection.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's well-meaning incompetence is on full display. His plan immediately has a logical flaw he can't see, which is entirely in character.

dialogue.speaker: Roxy
dialogue.line: and it's tighter than dick skin, man.

jokes.text: All right, check it out. You're gonna play my limo driver, right? You're just like a regular working stiff to this girl... Then we're out on the date and I'm like, 'Oh, I don't feel very well. I gotta go home. But let's not waste this date. Why don't you finish the date with my limo driver!'
jokes.setup: Charlie explains his dating scheme where he pretends to be a millionaire and Frank is the driver.
jokes.punchline: The plan — that a woman would enthusiastically agree to date the limo driver after the millionaire bails — is presented with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's harebrained scheme is specific and absurd in a way that's deeply Charlie — it kind of makes sense in a deranged way. The plan has its own internal logic, which is funnier than pure randomness.

dialogue.speaker: Roxy
dialogue.line: Screw your dick skin jacket, man. How do you like me now, gay boy?

jokes.text: Smart, Charlie. I mean, yeah, she's not gonna be able to resist an opportunity like that. A night with a limo driver?
jokes.setup: Charlie pitches his plan. Frank reacts.
jokes.punchline: Frank's sarcasm — or possibly sincerity — about the appeal of a limo driver is ambiguous and funny either way.
jokes.explanation: Light laugh from Frank's ambiguous delivery. 'A night with a limo driver?' as the thrilling payoff is a solid understated beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's Tiger Woods? Your life is way more glamorous than what I was picturing.

jokes.text: Oh, here, I think these are done. / That first one's done? / Yeah, this batch is done. / Just get 'em out. / Get 'em out -- whoo, baby! / Whoa! I burned myself on a rivet.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Frank are excitedly making plans.
jokes.punchline: They are boiling denim — confirming that this is an actual ongoing activity, mid-scene. Frank burns himself on a rivet.
jokes.explanation: One of the best visual/character jokes in the episode. The callback to the denim-boiling detail is now confirmed as an ACTIVE, ongoing activity — they are literally in the middle of doing it. 'I burned myself on a rivet' is the perfect injury from this absurd practice. Payoff on the earlier setup with strong escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Roxy
dialogue.line: Now, help me dig these crack rocks out of my ass.

jokes.text: Mac, these blood tests are going to show you the damage that you've been doing to your body, and my hope is that it will incentivize you to finally lose some of this disgusting weight you've put on.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are at a doctor's office.
jokes.punchline: Dennis frames a medical appointment as a confrontation and opportunity to shame Mac about his weight.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the medical scene. 'Incentivize' is a funny word choice — Dennis speaks about motivating Mac's health like a business problem.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I feel like I'm a four year old going to my sister's wedding.

jokes.text: No, I am going to look 20 forever, Mac, because the older I get, the more vigilant I become. All right, I don't eat lunch anymore. / Yeah, and on odd days, I don't eat breakfast. / That sounds miserable. / No, dude, it's not miserable. / Well, yeah, it is a little bit miserable, but it has to be.
jokes.setup: Mac pushes back that they can't look 20 forever.
jokes.punchline: Dennis describes his increasingly extreme diet regimen, then immediately admits it's miserable, but defends it anyway.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's vanity-fueled self-torture is funny — his partial self-awareness ('it is a little bit miserable, but it has to be') makes it richer than pure delusion. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Tarnation! You look as pretty as a peach.

jokes.text: I am also constantly in motion. Like, right now, dude, I am doing leg lifts that are imperceptible to the human eye. I call them hummingbirds. And although I seem relaxed, I'm actually incredibly tense at all times.
jokes.setup: Dennis is describing his fitness regimen.
jokes.punchline: He claims to be doing imperceptible leg exercises called 'hummingbirds' while appearing completely still — the name and the concept are both absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Hummingbirds' as a name for invisible leg lifts is specific, absurd, and completely believable as something Dennis Reynolds would invent and name. 'Although I seem relaxed, I'm actually incredibly tense at all times' is both a fitness claim and an accidental psychological self-portrait. Very high quotability — this is a cultural touchstone for Always Sunny fans. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: hustlin' and a-rasslin'. made a decent penny in boiled denims and, uh, the bridge business mostly.

jokes.text: Stop saying that. You are not cultivating mass, and if you are, stop cultivating and start harvesting.
jokes.setup: Mac insists he is 'cultivating mass,' not gaining fat.
jokes.punchline: Dennis extends the agricultural metaphor — if you're cultivating, it's time to harvest — meaning it's time to actually use/lose it.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever wordplay that extends Mac's euphemism on its own terms and uses it against him. 'Cultivating to harvesting' is an unexpected rhetorical move that's both funny and devastatingly logical. High quotability. Among the sharper wit jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I found a whole case of eggs under a bridge last week-- perfect condition. None of them missing. None of them cracked.

jokes.text: Try and move me, bro. / Wow, I'm not going to try... / Try and move me, bro.
jokes.setup: Mac wants to demonstrate his physical mass as proof he's strong, not fat.
jokes.punchline: Dennis wisely refuses; Mac insists — implying they then try it in the doctor's office.
jokes.explanation: The setup for a physical bit in a doctor's office. Mac's confidence and Dennis's reluctance are both in character.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Can I offer you a nice egg in this trying time?

jokes.text: Take a running start.
jokes.setup: Mac has told Dennis to try to move him. Dennis hesitates.
jokes.punchline: Mac ups the ante — giving Dennis a running start, in a doctor's office.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words that escalate the absurdity maximally. The implication that they then actually do this (interrupted by the doctor) is funnier than showing it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I swallowed, like, a million blood caplets 'cause I was gonna cough, like, you know, a handful of blood to make it real.

jokes.text: Excuse me. Did you want me to read these test results or not? / Yeah, I was just trying to... trying to move him. / He's like a brick wall.
jokes.setup: The doctor is trying to deliver test results while Mac and Dennis conduct a physical challenge.
jokes.punchline: The doctor's exasperated interruption and Dennis sincerely explaining he was 'trying to move him' — then Mac confirming his own brick wall status.
jokes.explanation: The doctor as straight man is well deployed. Dennis's earnest explanation to the doctor ('I was trying to move him') and Mac's satisfied self-description ('he's like a brick wall') both land.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: And I love boiling denim and banging whores! And I don't care if anybody doesn't like that about me.

jokes.text: I see severe dehydration, multiple vitamin deficiencies, anemia, low blood pressure. / Mac, look, I don't want you to fret... I'm going to get you on my exercise program. / Uh, these are your results, Mr. Reynolds.
jokes.setup: The doctor begins reading alarming test results; Dennis immediately volunteers his fitness program for Mac.
jokes.punchline: The results are actually Dennis's — the sick person is Dennis, not Mac.
jokes.explanation: One of the best structured jokes in the episode. The setup is perfectly misleading — Dennis spent the whole scene lecturing Mac about health, which makes the reversal more devastating. Dennis immediately volunteers his exercise program for Mac and then it's revealed it's Dennis who's dying. Textbook misdirection with strong character payoff. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I know who you are. This guy's an actor. He definitely pretended to be Donovan McNabb one time when I tried out for the Eagles.

jokes.text: I'm healthy as shit. / Well, uh, not according to your tests. / I'm healthier than you, bro. / Well, I wouldn't exactly say you're healthy. / You have type 2 adult-onset diabetes.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been told the terrible results are his.
jokes.punchline: Dennis insists he's healthy; Mac claims he's healthier than Dennis; then diabetes is revealed.
jokes.explanation: Mac's triumphant 'I'm healthier than you, bro' after spending the whole scene being body-shamed by Dennis is perfectly timed. The diabetes reveal lands hard as a button on the reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Fake Tiger Woods
dialogue.line: I'm busted. I am an actor. My name is Don Cheadle.

jokes.text: Type 2 adult-onset diabetes? What does that mean for me? / Well, that means you're going to have to inject yourself several times a day with insulin... / But I'm healthy besides the diabetes?
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes.
jokes.punchline: 'But I'm healthy besides the diabetes?' — Dennis immediately tries to establish a loophole in his diagnosis.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the episode. The specific phrasing 'healthy besides the diabetes' is both a denial mechanism and a logical impossibility. It's completely Dennis — he immediately tries to negotiate his way around reality. High quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Chimichanga, chimichanga, chimichanga, chimichanga, chimichanga.

jokes.text: I'm more healthier than he is, I think is the point that you're trying to make. Even with the diabetes.
jokes.setup: Dennis is reeling from his diabetes diagnosis while Mac was declared relatively healthier.
jokes.punchline: Mac tries to get the doctor to officially validate his superiority — specifically asking for confirmation 'even with the diabetes.'
jokes.explanation: Mac's competitive need to 'win' the health contest even in a doctor's office is perfectly in character. 'Even with the diabetes' is a great tag. The grammar error ('more healthier') is a small but authentic Mac touch.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What I really want?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Crack.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh. I thought you were gonna say pizza or buffalo wings or something.

jokes.text: Dude, stop saying 'diabetes!' You sound like an ass...
jokes.setup: Mac keeps saying the word 'diabetes' triumphantly.
jokes.punchline: Dennis, who has just been diagnosed with diabetes, tells Mac to stop saying the word 'diabetes' — as if the word is the problem.
jokes.explanation: Denial comedy — Dennis believes if Mac stops saying the word, the problem goes away. Classic Dennis vanity.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm still gonna pay you, but I want you to stop banging other guys. What do you say? Want to be my wife or what?

jokes.text: I'm fine. I just, uh... been doing a lot of hummingbirds today. I'm good.
jokes.setup: Dennis appears to have an episode — possibly a blood sugar crash from not eating — and the doctor asks if he's okay.
jokes.punchline: Dennis attributes his apparent health event to doing too many hummingbirds.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Dennis apparently just blood-sugar-crashed from not eating, and his explanation is 'too many hummingbirds.' The callback rewards attentive viewers and makes the earlier joke retroactively funnier. Character-specific, economical, and delivers the season's thesis about Dennis's self-destruction through vanity.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The bitch is dead! How could she be dead? I'm telling you her heart popped.

jokes.text: Have you eaten anything today? / No. / All right, let's get out of here, bro. I'm going to get you something to eat. / I'm going to lift you up. / What the hell? / I'm not as strong as I thought, Dennis. / Okay, I've hurt my back.
jokes.setup: Mac, fresh from claiming to be a 'brick wall,' tries to physically help Dennis up.
jokes.punchline: Mac cannot lift Dennis and hurts his back — immediately disproving his entire physical argument from the scene.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the medical scene — Mac's physical delusion is instantly debunked. 'I'm not as strong as I thought, Dennis' is a great line, delivered as genuine surprise. The callback to the brick wall claim makes it a satisfying payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Dead hooker in my apartment? That doesn't look good for me. I'm covered in blood.

jokes.text: I'm shit-faced. / Yeah, well, you downed that bottle of schnapps like it was a soda pop.
jokes.setup: Dee and Roxy are in a clothing store for the Pretty Woman makeover.
jokes.punchline: Roxy is already drunk; Dee reports how she got there, using the specific detail 'soda pop.'
jokes.explanation: 'Soda pop' is a funny, slightly dated word choice that makes the sentence funnier than it would be with just 'soda.' Establishes the chaos of the makeover scene.

dialogue.line: We could just put her out in the hall. We call in an anonymous tip.

jokes.text: Oh, and it's tighter than dick skin, man.
jokes.setup: Roxy is trying on a $500 jacket in a fancy store.
jokes.punchline: Her assessment of the jacket's fit uses a comparison that is both graphic and oddly specific.
jokes.explanation: 'Tighter than dick skin' as a fashion critique is pure Roxy — specific, crude, and oddly evocative. Only she would say this. High quotability through sheer specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I think Roxy would have wanted it that way.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, there you go.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Frank would know.

jokes.text: We're in a classy place with classy clothes for classy people, okay? Don't talk about dick skin.
jokes.setup: Roxy says 'tighter than dick skin' in a fancy store; Dee tries to manage her.
jokes.punchline: Dee's attempt to enforce decorum ends with the specific instruction 'Don't talk about dick skin' — which she now has to say out loud in the store.
jokes.explanation: The irony of saying 'don't talk about dick skin' as a command in a fancy store undermines Dee's decorum project. Callback to Roxy's line also. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Roxy, God bless you. You were a good whore. You serviced me like no other whore ever did. Not only my crank, but my heart.

jokes.text: Are you implying we can't afford that? / Can you? / That's none of your business. / Um, it's exactly my business.
jokes.setup: The store clerk asks if Dee and Roxy know the jacket costs $500.
jokes.punchline: Dee claims it's none of the store clerk's business whether they can afford the merchandise — which is exactly the store clerk's business.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pretty Woman reference playing out in real time. The clerk's flat 'it's exactly my business' is a perfect deadpan counter. This scene is building toward a subversion of the movie's famous beat.

jokes.text: Screw your dick skin jacket, man.
jokes.setup: The store clerk is being dismissive; Roxy decides to leave.
jokes.punchline: Roxy's exit insult connects the jacket back to her earlier 'dick skin' assessment — now weaponized as an insult.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the dick skin line, now repurposed as an insult hurled at the jacket. Economical and very much in Roxy's voice.

jokes.text: How do you like me now, gay boy? / Don't call him gay, 'cause it'd be one thing if he wasn't, but he clearly is, so...
jokes.setup: Roxy does something to the store clerk and taunts him.
jokes.punchline: Dee's correction is not 'don't call him gay' because it's offensive — it's 'don't call him gay because he clearly IS and that makes it weird.'
jokes.explanation: Dee's attempt at a sensitivity correction that immediately reveals she's not actually correcting the substance, just the optics — 'it'd be one thing if he wasn't, but he clearly is' is a funny distinction. Morally crooked in a way that's very Dee.

jokes.text: I'm trying to buy this coat, and this asshole here is giving me shit.
jokes.setup: Roxy has just yelled at and apparently assaulted the store clerk, then pivots to being the aggrieved customer.
jokes.punchline: Roxy frames herself as the victim of the encounter.
jokes.explanation: Roxy's total lack of self-awareness in casting herself as the victim is funny but not particularly original — a common comedy beat.

jokes.text: Oh, face, Jerry, face! Take a hike! / Sorry about the gay stuff. That did cross the line.
jokes.setup: Roxy has thrown money at the store manager and the clerk is dismissed.
jokes.punchline: Roxy gloats ('face!'); Dee apologizes specifically for the 'gay stuff' — not for any of the other chaos.
jokes.explanation: Dee's moral hierarchy — the 'gay stuff' crosses the line, but nothing else does — is a funny character note. The 'face!' celebration from Roxy is good energy.

jokes.text: You humiliated that salesman, and then you had the capital to back it up. I love you, Roxy.
jokes.setup: Roxy has thrown cash at the store; Dee now admires her.
jokes.punchline: Dee's declaration of love for Roxy is based entirely on Roxy's ability to humiliate a salesman with money — which is itself a Pretty Woman reference playing out as a dark inversion.
jokes.explanation: Dee's admiration is based on Roxy being crass and aggressive — which is the dark inversion of Pretty Woman's aspirational message. 'I love you, Roxy' as a conclusion to this chaos is funny.

jokes.text: Now, help me dig these crack rocks out of my ass.
jokes.setup: The makeover scene has apparently gone well; Dee is pleased.
jokes.punchline: Roxy asks for help retrieving crack she has stored in her body.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest Roxy lines. The abrupt pivot from the Pretty Woman triumph to 'help me dig these crack rocks out of my ass' is perfectly timed and absolutely destroys any romantic movie framing the scene had built. Highly quotable, strong punchline energy.

jokes.text: That's what I was picturing. / Yeah. / That's more like what I was picturing.
jokes.setup: Dee had mentally pictured Roxy's lifestyle differently.
jokes.punchline: After the 'crack rocks out of my ass' revelation, Dee confirms this is indeed what she expected — the Pretty Woman fantasy collapses instantly.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the crack line. The beat of Dee adjusting her expectations and then re-confirming them is a solid reaction moment.

jokes.text: Charlie, I feel like a sack of shit in this thing. / You look good. / I feel like I'm a four year old going to my sister's wedding.
jokes.setup: Frank is dressed as a limo driver for Charlie's dating scheme.
jokes.punchline: Frank's self-description — 'a four year old going to my sister's wedding' — is oddly specific and evocative, suggesting a comically ill-fitting formal outfit.
jokes.explanation: 'A four year old going to my sister's wedding' is a vivid, specific, and original simile for how uncomfortable and out-of-place he feels. The image is funny and human in a rare way for Frank.

jokes.text: Oh, hello. / Tarnation! You look as pretty as a peach. / Yes, you do!
jokes.setup: Charlie is playing 'Hoss Bonaventure, CEO' — a Texan millionaire — and greets his date.
jokes.punchline: His Texan affectation produces 'Tarnation!' and 'pretty as a peach' — cartooonishly stereotyped and delivered by Charlie, who is not Texan.
jokes.explanation: 'Tarnation!' is funny on its own as a commitment bit — Charlie going full cartoon Texan with zero self-awareness. 'Yes, you do!' as an affirmation of his own observation is a small extra beat.

jokes.text: Hoss Bonaventure, CEO.
jokes.setup: Charlie is introducing himself in his fake Texan millionaire persona.
jokes.punchline: The name 'Hoss Bonaventure' — which sounds both Western and vaguely French — is an absurdly constructed fake name.
jokes.explanation: 'Hoss Bonaventure' is a great character name — the collision of Western ('Hoss') and French-sounding ('Bonaventure') plus the mundane 'CEO' appended creates maximum absurdity in minimal syllables. Highly quotable, entirely original. This is the kind of naming that becomes a show's shorthand.

jokes.text: Now, he's the finest driver in all the land, so you gonna get on just fine with him. / Hi. / Hand down. Only say hello once. / He's nervous!
jokes.setup: Charlie introduces Frank as his limo driver; Frank tries to greet the date.
jokes.punchline: Charlie corrects Frank's etiquette ('hand down, only say hello once') while simultaneously making excuses ('he's nervous!') — the scheme is already falling apart.
jokes.explanation: 'Only say hello once' as an etiquette rule is funny because it suggests Frank said hello multiple times or waved too much. Charlie managing Frank while maintaining the persona is good cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, uh, well, uh, hustlin' and a-rasslin'. Uh, you know, this and that. Uh, made a decent penny in boiled denims and, uh, the bridge business mostly.
jokes.setup: The date asks Hoss Bonaventure how he made his fortune.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's explanation of his wealth sources includes 'boiled denims' and 'the bridge business' — callbacks to his real lifestyle presented as millionaire industries.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Charlie cannot invent a fake backstory because he only knows his own life — so his fictional millionaire fortune comes from 'boiled denims and the bridge business.' The callback is perfect, the character integration is total, and the specificity is devastating. This is what makes Always Sunny great — the world-building is so consistent that the callback rewards episode-long attention.

jokes.text: Frank up there, though, now, that man is rich in spirit. / He's rich in caricature.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to sell Frank as 'rich in spirit' while keeping him as a limo driver.
jokes.punchline: The date's flat correction — 'rich in caricature' — is a sharp, unexpected line that suggests she's already seeing through the whole thing.
jokes.explanation: 'Rich in caricature' is a genuinely witty line from an otherwise silent character. It reframes Frank perfectly and suggests the date is smarter than everyone's giving her credit for.

jokes.text: I found a whole case of eggs under a bridge last week -- perfect condition. None of them missing. None of them cracked. I mean, who in their right mind throws away a perfectly good case of eggs this day and age? I mean, it's a sick world, don't you think?
jokes.setup: The date mentions bridges; Frank sees an opportunity to relate.
jokes.punchline: Frank's contribution to the bridge discussion is a story about finding eggs under a bridge — another window into his actual lifestyle, delivered with genuine moral outrage about food waste.
jokes.explanation: Frank's bridge egg story is excellent character comedy — his moral outrage about wasted eggs while himself being a person who lives under bridges and finds food there is rich. 'Who in their right mind throws away a perfectly good case of eggs' as genuine philosophical indignation is very funny. 'It's a sick world' as the conclusion shows Frank has a consistent, if deranged, moral framework.

jokes.text: I got bit by a crab under that same bridge. / Oh, did you? / Yeah. You ever been bit by a crab, hon? / Can we maybe put this divider up?
jokes.setup: Frank has been sharing bridge stories; the date is visibly uncomfortable.
jokes.punchline: Frank escalates to being bitten by a crab, asks the date if she's ever been bitten by a crab, and the date's response is to ask for a physical barrier.
jokes.explanation: 'You ever been bit by a crab, hon?' as a conversational gambit on a blind date is a perfect Frank non-sequitur. The date's request for a divider as the punchline is a clean visual comedy beat — she wants a literal wall between herself and Frank.

jokes.text: Well, no, we don't want to exclude a great man like Frank from the conver... / Oh, my God! / Call 911! / No, it's okay. I have a touch of consumption. / He's all right.
jokes.setup: Charlie is about to fake being sick so Frank can take over the date.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a subtle fake illness, something dramatic happens; Charlie diagnoses himself with 'consumption' — a Victorian-era disease.
jokes.explanation: 'I have a touch of consumption' is a great line — 'consumption' as the chosen fake illness is an absurdly dated and theatrical choice, perfectly Charlie. 'He's all right' from Charlie immediately after this dramatic emergency is a good button.

jokes.text: I think I've been poisoned by my constituents! / Oh, my God! / Can I offer you a nice egg in this trying time?
jokes.setup: Charlie is performing a dramatic fake illness in the limo.
jokes.punchline: He claims to be 'poisoned by my constituents' (a politician's ailment, not a millionaire CEO's) while Frank offers an egg — presumably from the bridge case — as medical aid.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Poisoned by my constituents' is absurd in multiple ways — Charlie has broken character, used the wrong terminology (CEO, not politician), and the concept of being poisoned by constituents is deranged. Frank immediately offering a bridge egg 'in this trying time' as a remedy is a perfect callback. The juxtaposition of the emergency and the egg offer is excellent.

jokes.text: I swallowed, like, a million blood caplets 'cause I was gonna cough, like, a handful of blood to make it real. And now I'm thinking, like, you're not supposed to eat them or something 'cause they're making me really sick.
jokes.setup: Charlie explains why the fake illness went so wrong.
jokes.punchline: He consumed a large quantity of theatrical blood capsules and is now genuinely ill from it.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Charlie swallowed theatrical blood caplets to vomit blood as a 'realistic' touch — and then made himself actually sick — is a perfect Charlie story. His logic ('make it real') is sound in his world. 'You're not supposed to eat them or something' as his vague understanding of the product is very Charlie.

jokes.text: Aw, Charlie, you blew it. / You're the one talking about eggs and crabs and shit. / I love eggs, Charlie. I like eggs. And I love crabs. I like crabs. And I love boiling denim and banging whores! And I don't care if anybody doesn't like that about me.
jokes.setup: The date has fled; both Frank and Charlie blame each other.
jokes.punchline: Frank's self-defense escalates into a full declaration of his authentic self — eggs, crabs, boiling denim, and 'banging whores' — delivered as a proud manifesto.
jokes.explanation: One of the best moments in the episode. Frank's escalating self-affirmation — 'I love eggs. I love crabs. I love boiling denim and banging whores' — is a thesis statement for his character, delivered with complete sincerity and pride. The list structure builds perfectly, and 'banging whores' as the climax is unexpected despite being entirely consistent. High quotability, excellent callback integration, strong escalation structure.

jokes.text: I miss Roxy. / Yeah. / Roxy and I are made for each other.
jokes.setup: The date has fled; Frank reflects on his romantic life.
jokes.punchline: Frank's revelation, following his manifesto, is that the mainstream dating world cannot contain him — he belongs with Roxy.
jokes.explanation: Good emotional beat that follows naturally from the manifesto. 'Made for each other' is touching and sad in a Frank way.

jokes.text: Tiger Woods? / I cannot believe you invited him over here, Roxy. My place is a mess.
jokes.setup: Tiger Woods (or someone claiming to be) is coming to Dee's apartment.
jokes.punchline: Dee's concern about the visit is not that a client is coming to her home — it's that the place is a mess.
jokes.explanation: Light social comedy — Dee's vanity about her apartment overrides everything else. Standard Dee self-absorbtion.

jokes.text: Hello. / Who are you? / Tiger Woods. / Hey, Tiger. / Hey, girl.
jokes.setup: Someone arrives claiming to be Tiger Woods.
jokes.punchline: Dee's question 'who are you?' followed by a flat 'Tiger Woods' — the absurdity is in the matter-of-fact delivery of an impossible claim.
jokes.explanation: 'Hey, girl' as Tiger Woods's greeting to a room is funny in its casual cool. The scene is primarily setup for the reveal.

jokes.text: Of course you do, honey. I'm very famous.
jokes.setup: Dee says she knows who he is.
jokes.punchline: His confirmation of his own fame — 'I'm very famous' — delivered without irony, is overconfident and odd.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm very famous' is a funny line in context — it sounds like something a fraud would say to buttress their cover story.

jokes.text: Roxy, this is not Tiger Woods. / What are you talking about? / This guy's an actor. He definitely pretended to be Donovan McNabb one time when I tried out for the Eagles.
jokes.setup: Dee is confronting the fake Tiger Woods.
jokes.punchline: Dee's evidence is that he previously pretended to be Donovan McNabb when she 'tried out for the Eagles' — which reveals (a) she tried out for an NFL team and (b) this man has a history of celebrity impersonation for vulnerable people.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The specific detail that Dee 'tried out for the Eagles' — the NFL team — is a perfect character revelation. Dee's sad delusion about her athletic career is the real joke, with the celebrity impersonator's return being almost secondary. The specificity of Donovan McNabb makes it funnier than a generic QB.

jokes.text: Donovan McNabb? Eagles? I don't know what she's talking about. I play golf.
jokes.setup: Dee confronts the impersonator with his previous McNabb con.
jokes.punchline: He denies it by staying in character — 'I play golf' — as if that's a sufficient alibi.
jokes.explanation: 'I play golf' as a denial is funny — he's doubling down on the Tiger persona as his alibi. Good comic commitment.

jokes.text: All right, all right, I'm sorry. You got me, all right? I'm busted. I am an actor. My name is Don Cheadle.
jokes.setup: The impersonator is caught; he confesses.
jokes.punchline: His confession is that he's Don Cheadle — which is also not true, but he presents it as the genuine revelation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating absurdism — his 'confession' is simply a different lie. 'I am an actor. My name is Don Cheadle.' delivered with apparent sincerity after being 'busted' is brilliantly structured. The confidence of the pivot makes it land hard.

jokes.text: No, you're not Don... What are you doing?!
jokes.setup: The impersonator claims to be Don Cheadle.
jokes.punchline: Dee's bewildered reaction — cutting herself off mid-sentence to just ask 'What are you doing?!' — is a perfect straight-man response.
jokes.explanation: Dee's reaction is the right note — she doesn't argue the Don Cheadle claim, she just processes the insanity of the situation. Good reaction beat.

jokes.text: I don't care who he is if he pays me 500 bucks to rub my feet.
jokes.setup: Everyone is arguing about who this man actually is.
jokes.punchline: Roxy cuts through the entire existential debate with pure transactionalism — the identity question is irrelevant if he pays.
jokes.explanation: Roxy's pragmatism as a punchline cuts through the absurdity cleanly. The pivot to foot stuff as the specific service is a funny detail.

jokes.text: Hey, your feet are bizarrely huge. Man will go crazy for that. / I don't care for how you describe them, but what are we talking here?
jokes.setup: The fake Tiger/Don Cheadle examines Roxy's feet for a potential business arrangement.
jokes.punchline: He appraises her feet as 'bizarrely huge' — framing a potential insult as a business asset — and Roxy's response is to focus entirely on the money, not the description.
jokes.explanation: Roxy's negotiating position — 'I don't care for how you describe them, but what are we talking here?' — is a great character line. Pure business instinct.

jokes.text: Chimichanga, chimichanga, chimichanga, chimichanga, chimichanga.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are eating chimichangas.
jokes.punchline: Mac just says the word 'chimichanga' five times in a row with apparent relish.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Dennis's 'chimichanga' insult, now reclaimed by Mac as a joyful chant, is a good running gag beat. The repetition itself is the joke — Mac has completely embraced what was used as an insult.

jokes.text: Mac, chimichangas are delicious. / I told you, dude. / So good, oh! / I told you. / Why would you not want to eat one of these every single day of your life? / Oh, my God! / I mean, they're delicious, they're full of carbs, which is great for a pump.
jokes.setup: Dennis, who earlier body-shamed Mac and is now diabetic, is enthusiastically eating chimichangas.
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims carbs are 'great for a pump' — the same person who was lecturing about dieting is now justifying unlimited chimichanga eating.
jokes.explanation: The reversal of Dennis's earlier health obsession — now he's a diabetic eating carbs and calling it a 'pump' — is a great character payoff. The hypocrisy is complete and entirely believable for Dennis.

jokes.text: I want you to say to yourself, 'Chimichanga, you are delicious, but what do I really want?' / What I really want? / What do you want more than anything else in the entire world? / Crack. / Oh. I thought you were gonna say pizza or buffalo wings or something.
jokes.setup: Dennis has a philosophical approach to Mac's food choices — building toward some kind of insight about desire.
jokes.punchline: Mac's answer to 'what do you want more than anything in the world' is 'crack cocaine' — not food, not health, not success.
jokes.explanation: One of the best structured jokes in the episode. Dennis's inspirational framework is building toward a 'treat yourself' revelation; the actual answer — crack cocaine — is both a perfect subversion and completely in keeping with the episode's themes. 'I thought you were gonna say pizza or buffalo wings' as the expectation Dennis had is an excellent button, confirming he had no idea this was coming.

jokes.text: Now, I've never had crack. / Dude, you are going to love it. / I am? / It's so good. / Let's do it! / No restrictions, baby, no restrictions. / Aw, man, this is gonna be awesome, dude.
jokes.setup: Mac wants crack; Dennis has never tried it.
jokes.punchline: Dennis enthusiastically agrees to try crack cocaine for the first time, framed in his self-improvement philosophy: 'no restrictions.'
jokes.explanation: Dennis reframing first-time crack use as 'no restrictions, baby' in his self-improvement paradigm is a perfect dark comedy beat. The enthusiasm is what makes it — both characters sound like they're discussing a great brunch spot.

jokes.text: Do you want some insulin? / Oh, shit. / Yo.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are excitedly planning to do crack.
jokes.punchline: Mac remembers Dennis has diabetes and offers insulin — as a minor logistical aside before the crack.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of insulin and crack as sequential steps in a plan is excellent. 'Do you want some insulin?' asked with the same casual energy as 'want a beer?' is the joke. The 'Oh, shit' callback to the diabetes reveal as a sudden memory adds to it.

jokes.text: Dude, so, apparently, Charlie just puked blood all over some lady in a limousine and Dee is sucking off Don Cheadle or something? And Frank wants to go ahead and get married to Roxy as soon as possible.
jokes.setup: Mac gets a phone call and relays the information.
jokes.punchline: His summary of the other characters' current situations — blood vomit, Don Cheadle, and a sudden proposal — delivered flatly as if reading a grocery list.
jokes.explanation: The 'catch-up' speech that recontextualizes the episode's subplots as an absurd list is well-executed. 'Dee is sucking off Don Cheadle or something?' is particularly good — the 'or something' implies Mac isn't sure and doesn't entirely care.

jokes.text: Dude, we can get crack from Roxy. / Let's get crack from Roxy. / Okay, perfect.
jokes.setup: Mac reports that Frank wants to propose to Roxy; they need to go find them.
jokes.punchline: Their primary motivation for going is not to support Frank — it's to source crack from Roxy.
jokes.explanation: Their total self-interest in what should be a supportive moment is very Always Sunny. The brisk 'okay, perfect' as a plan is the right note.

jokes.text: On the way, let's fire down to John Wanamaker's and get ourselves a couple of Tommy Bahama shirts. Are you familiar?
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are about to go do crack for the first time.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's pre-crack priority is acquiring Tommy Bahama shirts at a department store, delivered with the gravity of a business proposition.
jokes.explanation: Tommy Bahama shirts as a first-crack-experience outfit is very specific and funny. 'Are you familiar?' is a great pompous tag line. The juxtaposition of Tommy Bahama and crack cocaine is well-mined.

jokes.text: Yeah, see what you mean about these shirts, bro. / Yeah. You'll grow into yours, buddy. / Yeah, comfy as shit. / They hide your fatness.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are now wearing Tommy Bahama shirts.
jokes.punchline: Dennis says Mac will 'grow into' his shirt — which is backwards (he means Mac should shrink to fit it) — then corrects course with 'they hide your fatness.'
jokes.explanation: 'They hide your fatness' as the actual selling point of Tommy Bahama shirts is a funny callback to the weight arc. Dennis's initial 'grow into' slip is a small extra beat.

jokes.text: Also, I'm gonna become a foot girl.
jokes.setup: Roxy is describing her new life direction.
jokes.punchline: Her 'second act' is pivoting her sex work specialty to feet — a callback to the foot fetish subplot.
jokes.explanation: Roxy's version of the 'second act' speech — framed as career development within sex work. 'Foot girl' is a perfectly funny euphemism. Good callback integration.

jokes.text: What's up, basticks? / Basticks? Is that how you're gonna talk from now on?
jokes.setup: Roxy greets the arriving gang.
jokes.punchline: 'Basticks' is apparently Roxy's new word — a portmanteau/corruption of 'bastards' — and Dennis immediately clocks it as a new verbal tic.
jokes.explanation: 'Basticks' is a good invented word — specific enough to be memorable, vague enough to be funny. Dennis's immediate noticing is the right reaction.

jokes.text: Roxy... you are good shit, and I want to make this legit. I'm still gonna pay you, but I want you to stop banging other guys. What do you say? Want to be my wife or what?
jokes.setup: Frank has gathered everyone for the proposal.
jokes.punchline: Frank's marriage proposal — 'you are good shit,' 'I'm still gonna pay you,' 'want to be my wife or what?' — is both romantic and completely Frank.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Frank moments in the episode. 'You are good shit' as a term of endearment, 'I'm still gonna pay you' as a marriage term, and 'want to be my wife or what?' as the actual question — this is a fully Frank Reynolds marriage proposal, completely in character. The payoff on the episode's main emotional thread.

jokes.text: The bitch is dead! / How could she be dead? / I'm telling you her heart popped.
jokes.setup: Roxy has just collapsed and died.
jokes.punchline: Mac's announcement ('the bitch is dead!') and Frank's medical explanation ('her heart popped') are both completely inappropriate and entirely consistent with these characters.
jokes.explanation: 'The bitch is dead!' and 'her heart popped' are both excellent lines — crude, specific, and character-perfect. 'Heart popped' as Frank's medical diagnosis is specifically Frank. High quotability on both lines.

jokes.text: Dead hooker in my apartment? That doesn't look good for me.
jokes.setup: Roxy has just died in Dee's apartment.
jokes.punchline: Dee's immediate concern is not grief or shock — it's how this looks for her.
jokes.explanation: 'That doesn't look good for me' as the first reaction to a person's death is a perfect Dee line — total self-absorption, appropriate horror, all in one. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: It would kind of mess up our second acts a little bit.
jokes.setup: The gang is debating what to do with the dead body.
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes the 'second act' framework — used earlier for earnest self-improvement discussion — to refer to the problem of having a dead prostitute.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the 'second act' philosophy, introduced as an earnest self-improvement concept, is now being applied to obstacle management after a death. The cold appropriation of the framework is funny.

jokes.text: And I'll tell you guys something. I smoked a little crack in the car on the way over. / Oh, you bitch! / Oh, does she still have any?
jokes.setup: Everyone is processing the death of Roxy.
jokes.punchline: Dee admits she smoked some of Roxy's crack; Mac is outraged — but Dennis's outrage is immediately revealed to be about wanting the remaining crack.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured two-beat joke. Mac's 'oh, you bitch!' sounds like moral outrage — then Dennis immediately undercuts it with 'oh, does she still have any?' The misdirection is tight and the character work is excellent. One of the funnier moments in the third act.

jokes.text: I don't want to sound insensitive, but we could just put her out in the hall. We call in an anonymous tip. So we're still calling 911... Someone finds her. ...just from a pay phone.
jokes.setup: The gang debates what to do with the body.
jokes.punchline: Their plan — dump the body in the hall, call 911 from a pay phone — is presented with the preamble 'I don't want to sound insensitive.'
jokes.explanation: 'I don't want to sound insensitive' before proposing to dump a body in a hallway is a classic Always Sunny politeness-before-amorality beat. 'From a pay phone' as the detail that makes it legitimate in their minds is funny.

jokes.text: Frank, what do you think? / I think Roxy would have wanted it that way. / Well, there you go. Frank would know.
jokes.setup: The gang defers to Frank on what to do with Roxy's body.
jokes.punchline: Frank's ruling — 'Roxy would have wanted it that way' — refers to being left in a hallway; Mac and Dennis accept this as authoritative.
jokes.explanation: 'Roxy would have wanted it that way' applied to being dumped in a hallway is a good dark comedy beat. The funeral-language applied to a disposal plan is the irony. 'Frank would know' as an authoritative ratification is a good button.

jokes.text: Roxy, God bless you. You were a good whore. You serviced me like no other whore ever did. Not only my crank, but my heart. And I'm gonna miss ya.
jokes.setup: Frank has asked to say a few words over Roxy's body before they put her in the hallway.
jokes.punchline: His eulogy — 'you were a good whore,' 'you serviced my crank AND my heart' — is simultaneously the most and least appropriate funeral speech ever given.
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. Frank's eulogy for Roxy hits every note perfectly: 'You were a good whore' (crude but sincere), 'serviced my crank, but my heart' (the 'crank/heart' construction is a brilliant double entendre used earnestly), and 'I'm gonna miss ya' as the genuine emotional close. This is the culmination of the entire episode's dark romantic thread. The structure — crude → cruder → genuinely touching — is exceptional. Comparable to the Snip Snap anchor in terms of character-specific emotional comedy. Frank's affection for Roxy, expressed entirely in his own language, is both funny and oddly moving. Among the strongest jokes in the series.

jokes.text: So should we get the dead whore out of the apartment? / Yeah, yeah, yeah.
jokes.setup: Frank has just finished his eulogy; there is a solemn moment.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately snaps back to logistics: 'So should we get the dead whore out of the apartment?'
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the entire episode. The pivot from Frank's sincere eulogy back to the practical problem — in the most blunt possible language — captures the show's ethos completely. Good economical closer.

jokes.text: So should we get the dead whore out of the apartment? / Yeah, yeah, yeah.
jokes.setup: The eulogy has concluded; a brief moment of silence.
jokes.punchline: Mac returns to practical logistics with 'So should we get the dead whore out of the apartment?' — a perfect deflation of the preceding emotional peak.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button for the episode. After Frank's moving/grotesque eulogy, the return to logistics is exactly right. The word 'So' at the start implies a reasonable amount of time has passed for reflection. Good economy — this line does its job entirely.

tmdb_overview: With Frank intent on marrying a prostitute, The Gang tries to make the best of it by attempting an image makeover to uncover the heart of gold that exists deep inside Frank’s “pretty woman.”
